Surah al-Muzzammil is Meccan, except for verses ten, eleven, and twenty, which are Medinan. Its verses number twenty.

﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾. That is, the one who wraps himself in his garments when he draws them around himself. The *ta'* is assimilated into the *zay* (*idgham*, the merging of one consonant into the next), and it has also been read in its original form. It has been read as *al-muzammal* (with the *mim* doubled and the *zay* vowelled with a fatha, the passive form), derived from *zamalahu*, and also in the active form. It is said that the Prophet (ﷺ) was addressed in this way to reproach the state he was in, for he (peace be upon him) was wrapped in a cloak, prepared for sleep, as one does who has no concern and no urgent matter. He was therefore commanded to abandon wrapping himself up in order to rise up for worship and to pass the night in *tahajjud* (voluntary night prayer). It is also said that the Prophet (peace be upon him) entered upon Khadijah (may Allah be pleased with her) while trembling with fear, at the first time Jibril (peace be upon them both) came to him, and his shoulders were quivering. He said: "Wrap me up, wrap me up," and she supposed that something had come upon him. While he was in that state, Jibril called to him and said: "O you who are wrapped up." In that case, the specifying of the attribute of wrapping in the address is for gentleness and reassurance, as in the words of the Prophet (peace be upon him) to ʿAli (may Allah be pleased with him) when he had angered Fatimah (may Allah be pleased with her): when he came to him while he was asleep and dust had stuck to his side, he said: ﴿Arise, O Father of Dust﴾, as a gentle address and to show that he was not reproaching him. It is also said that the meaning is: O you who has been burdened (*zummila*) with a great matter, namely the matter of prophethood, that is, bearing it. *Al-zaml* means a load, and *izdamalahu* means he carried it. In that case, mentioning the attribute here indicates that it is the reason for rising up or for being commanded to do so, for bearing the burdens of prophethood (peace be upon him) is something that necessitates striving diligently in worship.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 73, verse 2:

﴿Stand [in prayer] through the night﴾ That is: stand up for the prayer. The accusative of "the night" (al-layl) is adverbial of time (ẓarfiyyah). It has also been said: "standing" (al-qiyam) is used figuratively for prayer, and the meaning of "qum" is "pray." It has been recited with a ḍammah and with a fatḥah on the mīm (qumi / qum).

﴿Except a little﴾ This is an exception from "the night." And His, may He be exalted, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 73, verse 3:

﴿Half of it﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "the night" that remains after the exception, a substitute of the whole (badal al-kull); that is, "Stand (in prayer) for half of it." The expression of the half that is singled out as "little" serves to show the full regard for the part that is coupled with standing (in prayer) and to signal its excellence, and the standing in it is treated as standing in most of it with respect to the abundance of reward. Considering its smallness relative to the whole, while it is devoid of benefit, is contrary to the apparent meaning.

﴿Or reduce from it﴾, i.e., reduce the standing from the half coupled with it in the first case. (p-50)﴿a little﴾, i.e., a slight reduction, or a small amount, such that it does not descend to half of the half.

﴿Or add to it﴾: that is, add to the standing over the half that accompanies it. The meaning is that he (ﷺ) was given the choice between standing for half the night, or less than it, or more than it.

It has been said that His saying, exalted is He, "half of it" (*nisfahu*) is a *badal* (apposition or substitute) for *qalilan* ("a little"), and that the choice remains as it is. But this is not sound. First, because the part deserving of attention, which the *badal* indicates, is the remainder after the exception, the portion that accompanies the standing, not the excluded portion that is bare of it. Second, because the decrease and increase of the standing are measured against their standard, which is the half that accompanies it. So if *nisfahu* were made a *badal* of *qalilan*, it would require measuring the decrease and increase of the standing against what is entirely devoid of it. The excuse of the equality of the two halves, although it is an evident contrivance, is an acknowledgment that the first view is the correct one.

It has been said that *nisfahu* is a *badal* from *al-layl* ("the night"), and that *illa qalilan* is an exception (*istithna'*) from the half. The pronouns in *minhu* and *alayhi* refer to the half. The meaning is then a choice between two matters: to stand for less than half the night definitively, or to choose one of two options, namely a decrease from the half or an increase over it.

It has been said that the two pronouns refer to the lesser of the half, as if it were said: stand for less than half of it, or stand for less than that lesser amount, or for a little more than it. It has also been said that what befits the eloquence of the revelation is the first view. God knows best what is in His Noble Book.

﴿And recite the Qur'an﴾: and during what has been mentioned of standing (in prayer), that is, read it slowly and with clear distinction of the letters.

﴿With measured recitation (tartīlan)﴾: eloquent, such that the listener can count its words. This is from their saying, "a *thaghr ratal* and *ratil*," when the teeth are spaced apart (*mufallaj*).

﴿Indeed We shall cast upon you﴾, i.e., We shall reveal to you. The choice of "casting" (*al-ilqa'*) upon him is due to His saying ﴿a heavy word﴾, which is the Great Qur'an, containing arduous obligations that are heavy upon those who are charged, especially upon the Messenger (ﷺ), for he is commanded to bear them and to convey them to the community. The sentence is a parenthetical clause (*i'tiraḍ*) placed between the command and its rationale (*ta'lil*), explaining why the Messenger (ﷺ) is made to bear the command to stand in prayer. It was said that the meaning of its being heavy is: it is weighty (*rasin*) because of the solidity of its wording and the firmness of its meaning; or it is heavy upon the one who reflects on it, since it requires greater purification of the inner heart and detachment of the gaze; or it is heavy in the balance (on the Day of Judgment); or it is heavy upon the disbelievers and the wicked; or its receiving is heavy.

From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "When revelation came down to him, it weighed heavily upon him and his skin would take on a darkened hue." And from 'Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her: "I saw revelation coming down upon him on an extremely cold day, and when it departed from him, his forehead would be streaming with sweat."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 73, verse 6:

﴿Indeed, the rising of the night﴾ That is: indeed, the soul that rises from its resting place to worship, i.e., it stands up, from "nasha'a" (to rise) from his place when he gets up. Or, indeed, the standing in the night, with "al-nashi'a" being a verbal noun from "nasha'a," like "al-'afiyah." Or, indeed, the worship that arises (tansha' bi-al-layl) at night, i.e., it occurs. Or, indeed, the hours of the night, for they occur one after another, or its first hours, from "nasha'a" meaning "began."

﴿It is stronger in trampling﴾ That is: it is more firmly established in footing or more burdensome; therefore one must give attention to standing (in prayer). It has been read as "wiṭā'an" (wiṭā'), meaning: more conducive to harmonization, where the heart harmonizes with the tongue if by it is meant the soul, or where the heart of the one standing harmonizes with his tongue in it if by it is meant the standing, or the worship, or the hours; or more in agreement with what is intended of humility (khushu') and sincerity (ikhlas). ﴿And more upright in speech﴾ and more correct in utterance and more firmly established in recitation, because of the presence of the heart and the stillness of voices.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 73, verse 7:

﴿Indeed, for you by day there is extensive occupation.﴾ That is: constant turning about and busying yourself with your important affairs, and being preoccupied with your concerns, so that you cannot devote yourself fully to worship. So devote yourself to it at night. This is a clarification of the external motive for standing in prayer at night, after the clarification of the motive within oneself. It is also read as (sabkhan), meaning the scattering of the heart through preoccupations, a metaphor drawn from (sabkh al-suf) (the carding of wool), which is teasing out and spreading its fibers.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 73, verse 8:

﴿And mention the name of your Lord﴾, and persist in remembering Him, the Exalted, by night and by day, in whatever manner it may be, through glorification (tasbih), declaring His oneness (tahlil), praising Him (tahmid), prayer, recitation of the Qur'an, and the study of knowledge.

﴿And devote yourself to Him with devotion﴾. That is: separate yourself unto Him with the full concentration of your resolve and the complete absorption of your determination in watching over Him. Since this could not be achieved except by stripping himself, upon him be blessings and peace, of the obstacles that prevent one from watching over God, the Exalted, and by severing all ties to other than Him, it is said that ﴿tabtilan﴾ is used in place of (tabattulan), together with the observance of the rhyme (fawasil) it involves.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 73, verse 9:

﴿Lord of the East and the West; there is no god but He﴾ is in the nominative (marfu') by way of praise (al-madh), and it has been said: it is in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence (al-ibtida'), its predicate being ﴿there is no god but He﴾. It was also read in the genitive (majrur), as a substitute (badal) for "your Lord." It has been said: it is in the genitive by the implied particle of oath (idmar harf al-qasam), and its answer (jawab) is "there is no god but He." The fa' in His words, exalted is He, ﴿so take Him as a trustee (wakil)﴾ indicates the sequence of the command (li-tartib al-amr), and what necessitates it is the exclusivity of divinity (al-uluhiyya) and lordship (al-rububiyya) to Him, exalted is He.

**Verse 10:** ﴿Be patient over what they say﴾, of the idle talk in which there is no good.

﴿And forsake them with a gracious forsaking﴾, by keeping away from them, dealing with them tactfully, not repaying them in kind, and leaving their affairs to their Lord, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates:

Qur'anic quotations keep the ﴿ ﴾ markers; the passage is short and contains no hadith or poetry.

﴿And leave Me with those who deny⁠—﴾ that is: leave them to Me, and entrust their affair to Me, for I will suffice you against them.

﴿The people of luxury﴾: those lords of ease and comfort, and they are the chieftains of Quraysh.

﴿And give them respite, a little while﴾: a brief period of time.

﴿Indeed, with Us are shackles﴾ (ankal), the plural of nikl, which is a heavy fetter. The clause is an explanation (ta'lil) for the command; that is, indeed with Us are matters opposed to their luxurious living, ﴿and a blazing fire﴾ (jahim).

"And a food that chokes in the throat" — it sticks in the throats and can hardly be swallowed, like ḍarīʿ (a thorny, poisonous plant) and zaqqūm (a bitter tree of Hell).

"And a painful punishment" — and another kind of punishment, painful, whose measure cannot be estimated and whose true nature cannot be grasped. All of this is prepared and kept in readiness for them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 73, verse 14:

(p-52) And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the day when the earth and the mountains quake, and the mountains become a heap of loose sand, poured forth.﴾

﴿On the day when the earth and the mountains quake﴾, i.e., they are agitated and shaken. It is an adverbial of time (zarf) for the stationing (istiqrar) that is attached to "with Us" (ladayna). It has also been said that it is attached to an implied verb which is a description of "Our punishment," i.e., a punishment that will befall on the day when they quake.

﴿And the mountains were﴾, despite their firmness and height, ﴿a heap of sand﴾ (kathib), a gathered mass of sand, derived from kathaba al-shay'un (kathaba) when he gathered it. It is as if it is a fa'il in the sense of maf'ul (i.e., "gathered").

﴿Poured forth﴾ (mahil), scattered, from hala yahilu hailan when it is scattered and made to flow.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 73, verse 15:

﴿Indeed, We have sent to you﴾ O people of Mecca.

﴿a messenger, a witness against you﴾ who will testify on the Day of Resurrection to what proceeded from you of disbelief and disobedience.

﴿as We sent to Pharaoh a messenger﴾ He is Musa (peace be upon him), and the non-specification of him is because he has no bearing on the comparison.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 73, verse 16:

﴿But Pharaoh disobeyed the Messenger﴾, who We had sent to him. The place of the kaf (ك, "like," the kaf of comparison) is in the accusative, on the basis that it is an attribute (sifah) of a deleted verbal noun (masdar). That is: We sent to you a Messenger, and you disobeyed him, as His Exalted saying indicates: ﴿a witness over you﴾, a sending (irsalan) existing in the manner in which We sent to Pharaoh a messenger, and he disobeyed him. His Exalted saying: ﴿So We seized him with a severe seizing﴾ is outside the realm of comparison; it was brought for the purpose of alerting that what befell those (Pharaoh's people) will inevitably befall these (the Meccans) as well. Al-wabil (وبيل) means heavy and coarse, from the saying of the people "kala'un wabil" (a heavy pasture), meaning harmful, not agreeable to digest because of its heaviness. Al-wabil also means a huge staff.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 73, verse 17:

﴿Then how will you guard yourselves﴾ — that is, how will you protect your own selves?

﴿If you disbelieve﴾: that is, if you remain upon disbelief.

﴿A Day﴾ — that is, the punishment of a Day.

﴿That will make the children grey-haired﴾ — from the intensity of its terror and the awfulness of the calamities within it. ﴿Grey-haired﴾ (shuyban) is the plural of ashyab (grey-haired), either literally or figuratively. Its origin is that when worries and sorrows multiply upon a person, his strength weakens and grey hair quickly appears on him. It has also been permitted that this is a description of the Day as being long, but that is not the case.

﴿The sky is split asunder﴾: i.e., it is split open (munshaqq). It is also read *mutafattir*, meaning cracking (mutashaqqiq). The masculine form is used because the adjective is applied to a masculine noun that is described, i.e., a masculine thing that is split (shay'un munfaṭir). He referred to the sky in this way to draw attention to the fact that its reality has changed and its name and form have departed from it, so that nothing remains of it except what can be called "a thing." It has also been said that the masculine form is used because the sky is interpreted as the roof. It has also been said that this is of the category of *nisba* (relative adjectives, formed by adding a suffix to a noun), meaning "possessing splitting." The *bāʾ* in ﴿with it﴾ is like the *bāʾ* in *fuṭirat al-ʿūd bi-l-qadūm* (the wood was split with the adze).

﴿His promise is ever fulfilled﴾: the pronoun refers to God, Exalted and Majestic, and the verbal noun (*maṣdar*) is annexed to its agent. Alternatively, the pronoun refers to the Day, and the verbal noun is annexed to its object.

This is the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 73, verse 19:

﴿Indeed, this﴾ is a reference to the verses containing the calamities mentioned.

﴿is a reminder﴾ an admonition.

﴿So whoever wills takes a path to his Lord﴾ by drawing near to Him through faith and obedience, for these are the path (minhaj) that leads to His good pleasure.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 73, verse 20:

﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand in prayer almost two-thirds of the night﴾, i.e., less than them. The word "adna" (nearer, less) is used figuratively for this, because when the distance between two things decreases, the space between them becomes smaller. ﴿And half of it and a third of it﴾, in the accusative, as a conjunction with "adna". They were also read in the genitive, as a conjunction with "thulthay al-layl" (two-thirds of the night).

﴿And a group of those with you﴾, i.e., a group of your companions stands in prayer with you.

﴿And Allah determines the night and the day﴾. No one at all is able to determine them but He. The placing of the Majestic Name first makes it the subject (mubtada'), and the construction of "yuqaddiru" upon it necessarily implies exclusivity (ikhtisas), as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He knew that you would not be able to keep count of it﴾, i.e., He knew that you would certainly not be able to determine the times, and you would never be able to keep track of the hours.

﴿So He turned to you [in mercy]﴾, by permitting you to abandon the prescribed standing in prayer, and by removing the burden of blame from you for abandoning it.

﴿So recite what is easy of the Qur'an﴾, i.e., pray what is easy for you of the night prayer. He expressed prayer by recitation, just as He expressed it by its other pillars. It is said that the tahajjud (night prayer) was obligatory by the option mentioned, but it became difficult for them to stand for it, so it was abrogated by it (naskh, abrogation). Then this was abrogated by the five daily prayers. It is also said that it is the recitation of the Qur'an itself. They said: whoever recites one hundred verses of the Qur'an in a night will not be counted among those who argue against him (on the Day of Judgment). It was also said: whoever recites one hundred verses is recorded among the devout (qanitin), and it is said: fifty verses.

﴿He knows that there will be among you those who are sick﴾. This is a resumed statement (isti'naf) explaining another wisdom that calls for the permission and lightening.

﴿And others travelling through the land﴾, i.e., journeying in it for trade.

﴿Seeking of Allah's bounty﴾, which is profit. The seeking of bounty has been generalized to include seeking knowledge. ﴿And others fighting in the way of Allah﴾. When the matter is as mentioned, and the motives for permission converge, ﴿then recite what is easy of it﴾, without undertaking hardships.

﴿And establish the prayer﴾, i.e., the obligatory prayer.

﴿And give the zakat﴾, the obligatory alms. It is said that it is the zakat al-fitr, since there was no zakat in Makkah. Whoever interprets it as the obligatory zakat holds that the end of the surah is Madani.

﴿And lend to Allah a goodly loan﴾. It means spending in the ways of good, or paying zakat in the best and most beneficial manner to the poor.

﴿And whatever good you send forward for yourselves﴾, i.e., any good, whether of what has been mentioned or what has not been mentioned.

﴿You will find it with Allah, better and greater in reward﴾ than what you delay until the bequest at death. "Khayran" is the second object of "tajidu", and it is an emphatic or a separating pronoun (fasl), even though it does not fall between two definites, since "af'al min" is treated as definite, and therefore it is not prefixed with the article. It was also read "huwa khayrun" as a beginning and predicate.

﴿And seek forgiveness of Allah﴾ in all your circumstances, for a person is rarely free from negligence.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Muzzammil, Allah will remove hardship from him in this world and the next."
